blocks.prompt: The Walrus That Walks on Its Teeth
blocks.text: A walrus is heavy. It can weigh more than a small car. Its two long tusks are really teeth. They keep growing all its life. The walrus uses them like hooks. It hooks them into the ice and pulls itself up out of the water. That is why scientists call it the tooth walker. The walrus has hundreds of whiskers. It is dark at the bottom of the sea, so it feels for clams with its whiskers. Then it sucks the clam right out of the shell.

blocks.prompt: The Tooth Walker
blocks.text: Every walrus has two tusks, and every tusk is a tooth. They are the walrus's upper canine teeth, grown long. A big male's tusks can be as long as your arm, and they never stop growing. People used to think the walrus dug up its dinner with those tusks. It does not. The walrus hunts in the dark, on the muddy floor of a cold sea. It plows through the mud with its snout and feels around with its whiskers. A walrus has as many as seven hundred whiskers, and they are so sensitive that it can pick out one clam by touch alone. Then comes the strange part. The walrus does not crack the shell. It puts its mouth over the clam, pulls its tongue back like a piston, and sucks the soft body straight out. It leaves the empty shell behind. One hungry walrus can eat thousands of clams in a single trip to the bottom. So what are the tusks for? Hooks. A walrus jabs them into the ice and hauls its huge body up out of the freezing water.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Changes Color
blocks.text: A walrus hauled out on the ice in the Arctic wind looks almost white, or a dull pale gray. Watch the same animal an hour later, warm in the sun, and it has turned a deep rosy pink. Nothing has been painted. The walrus is moving its own blood. Under a walrus's wrinkled hide lies a layer of blubber that can be six inches thick. That fat is superb insulation, which is a problem when the animal gets too warm, because the heat has nowhere to go. So the walrus opens up the blood vessels in its skin and floods them. Warm blood rushes to the surface, sheds heat into the air, and the animal blushes. In cold water it does the reverse, shutting those vessels down and pulling its blood deep inside where the heat is needed. The color is a thermostat you can see. The walrus keeps a second surprise in its throat. It has two stretchy pouches there that it can fill with air, like blowing up a pair of balloons under its chin. Inflated, they hold the animal's head above the water while the rest of it hangs down, asleep and upright, a ton of walrus bobbing in the swell. Males also use the pouches to make a deep bell-like note that carries for miles underwater during the mating season. Even the tusks do double duty. They are hooks for climbing onto ice, weapons in a fight, and a rank badge. In a herd, the walrus with the longest tusks generally gets the best spot.

blocks.prompt: The Tooth Walker Runs Out of Ice
blocks.text: Odobenus rosmarus, the walrus, carries its name in its mouth. Odobenus is Greek for tooth walker, and the animal earns it: a walrus drives its tusks into the edge of an ice floe and levers a body weighing up to a ton and a half up out of the water. The tusks are elongated canine teeth, present in both males and females, and they grow for as long as the animal lives. Almost everything about a walrus is built around cold, dark water and the mud beneath it. Its eyes are weak and it barely uses them to hunt. Instead it carries four hundred to seven hundred vibrissae, the stiff whiskers fanned across its muzzle, each one wired to a dense bundle of nerves. A walrus can identify a buried clam by touch in total darkness, on a seafloor stirred to soup. It does not chew. It seals its lips around the shell, retracts its tongue like a piston, and the suction strips the animal out whole. A single walrus may empty several thousand shells in one feeding dive and surface with nothing to show for it. Walruses are not solitary. They pile onto ice floes in the hundreds, calves tucked among adults, sleeping in heaps and bellowing. That ice is not a luxury. It is a resting platform that floats directly above the shallow shelf where the clams are, which means a mother can dive, feed, and return to her calf without swimming for a day. Now the ice is going. In warm years the summer sea ice retreats north past the edge of the shelf, over water too deep to feed in, and the herds have nowhere to rest offshore. They come ashore instead, tens of thousands of animals crowded onto a single beach. On land they are jumpy. A plane, a bear, a noise, and the herd stampedes for the water, and the calves at the middle of it are crushed. Humans have taken walruses for at least a thousand years. Arctic peoples used the meat, the oil, and hides tough enough to stretch over a boat frame, and Norse traders shipped walrus ivory to Europe, where it was carved into crucifixes and chess pieces. Commercial hunting in the eighteen and nineteen hundreds nearly finished the Atlantic population. It survived. The ice may not.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Odobenus: Greek for tooth walker
Vibrissae rival primate fingertips for touch
Suction feeding: the tongue works like a piston
Blubber up to six inches thick
Skin blood flow is a visible thermostat
Chukchi summer ice now retreats past the shelf

blocks.prompt: The Tooth Walker and the Disappearing Floor
blocks.text: Consider the problem a walrus has to solve. Its food is buried in mud on the floor of the Arctic shelf, in water a few hundred feet deep and black as ink. Its body weighs as much as a small car and rarely stays under for more than about ten minutes. And it is warm-blooded in water near freezing. Every strange thing about a walrus is an answer to that problem. Start with the whiskers. A walrus has poor eyesight and does not much care, because it hunts by touch. Several hundred vibrissae fan out across its muzzle, each stiff bristle rooted in a bundle of nerves and blood so rich that a walrus's sense of touch rivals a primate's fingertips. Down in the dark, the animal plows its snout through sediment and blasts jets of water from its mouth to loosen the mud, and it reads what surfaces. Finding a clam is not the hard part. Opening it is. A walrus does not chew, and it does not crack the shell. It clamps its lips around the seam, hauls its huge tongue backward like a piston in a cylinder, and the vacuum that follows pulls the clam bodily out of its own house. The shell drops back to the mud, empty. In one bout of feeding a walrus may do this several thousand times. Then the cold. Blubber up to six inches thick wraps the animal, which solves the freezing problem and creates the opposite one: a walrus hauled out on ice in the sun has no easy way to dump heat. So it uses its skin as a radiator it can switch on. Chilled, a walrus shunts blood away from the surface and goes pale, almost ghostly gray. Warmed, it opens those vessels wide and floods them, and the herd on the ice turns a startling rosy pink. You can read a walrus's temperature from a helicopter. And the tusks. They are not digging tools, whatever the old books say. They are canines, they grow throughout life, and both sexes carry them. A walrus hooks them over the lip of a floe and levers a ton of itself out of the sea, which is why zoologists named the genus Odobenus, the tooth walker. Tusks are also a resume. In a crowded haul-out, the animal with the longest ivory takes the best position, usually without a fight, because everyone can see the argument already. All of this hangs on one thing that has nothing to do with anatomy: ice in the right place. Walruses feed on the continental shelf, where the water is shallow enough to reach. Sea ice drifting over that shelf gives a mother a floating bed directly above the pantry. She dives, she feeds, she surfaces to her calf. The ice does the commuting for her. For the last two decades the summer ice over the Chukchi shelf has retreated north into water thousands of feet deep, far past anything a walrus can dive. The herds are left with one option, and they take it: they come ashore. Haul-outs of tens of thousands of animals now form on Alaskan and Russian beaches where none used to be. Packed that tightly, a walrus is fragile. A low aircraft or a wandering bear panics the herd, it pours toward the water in a wall of bodies, and the calves in the middle do not come out. Biologists counting the dead after these stampedes find them by the hundreds. The tooth walker is a specialist, and specialists are precise instruments. This one is beautifully solved for a world with ice above the mud. We are removing the ice, and no amount of whisker, tusk, or blubber answers that.
